Published Nov 20, 2024, updated Feb 08, 2025 6 min CNC machining is a cornerstone of modern manufacturing. It's a process that allows industries to produce precise, complex parts with a level of consistency that would be hard to achieve with traditional methods. But what exactly are CNC parts, and how are they made? Let's break it down in a way that's easy to understand, so whether you're a DIY enthusiast or part of a business looking to create custom parts, you'll know how CNC machining can benefit you. What Exactly Are CNC Parts? In simple terms, CNC parts are components made by Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machines. These machines are controlled by computers that follow a set of precise instructions, allowing them to carve or mill a raw material—whether it's metal , plastic , or composite materials —into the exact shape needed. The magic happens with CAD (Computer-Aided Design) software. Designers create a 3D model of the part they need, and that design is then translated into G-code , which tells the CNC machine exactly what to do. From there, the CNC machine gets to work, automatically producing parts with incredible accuracy. How Are CNC Parts Made? Here's the step-by-step process of how CNC parts come to life: Designing the Part The first step in making any CNC part is the design. Using CAD software , you or your design team create a detailed model of the part. This could be a simple bracket, or something more intricate like a custom gear. Once the design is complete, it's converted into G-code , a language that the CNC machine can understand. Setting Up the CNC Machine With the design ready, it's time to set up the CNC machine. This involves loading the material, whether it's a block of aluminum , steel , plastic , or any other material, and securing it in place. Next, the machine's tools are loaded (cutters, drills, etc.), and the G-code is programmed into the system. The Machining Process Now for the fun part—the machining! The CNC machine starts working, following the G-code to precisely cut, mill, or drill the material into the shape of the part. This is done in stages, removing material layer by layer until the part takes shape. Whether it's milling , turning , or drilling , each operation is designed to achieve the most accurate result. Finishing Touches After the main machining is complete, the part may need a little polishing, deburring, or surface finishing to smooth out rough edges or to add a special coating. This ensures that the part functions perfectly while also having a polished, professional appearance. Why Are CNC Parts So Important? CNC parts are important because they provide a level of precision and adaptability that traditional manufacturing methods simply can't achieve. Here's why they're so crucial: Precision CNC machines are incredibly precise, making them perfect for parts that need to fit together perfectly. Whether you're creating a single prototype or manufacturing parts at scale, CNC machining guarantees each component is made to precise specifications. Flexibility Across Materials CNC machining isn't limited to just one type of material. CNC machines can handle a wide variety of materials—metals like aluminum , titanium , or stainless steel , as well as plastics like ABS and nylon . This flexibility makes CNC a great option for almost any type of project. Custom Designs One of the key advantages of CNC machining is its ability to create custom parts . If you need a unique component or have a specific design in mind, CNC gives you the flexibility to create exactly what you need, with no need for expensive molds or tooling. Efficiency Once a CNC machine is set up, it can run with minimal human intervention, often running for hours or even days on end. This efficiency makes CNC machining ideal for both low-volume runs and high-volume production, saving time and reducing labor costs. Where Can You Find CNC Parts? CNC parts are everywhere around us, even in places you might not immediately think of. Here are a few industries and areas where CNC machining plays a key role: Automotive Industry : Whether it's a custom suspension component or a high-precision engine block, CNC machines are behind many of the critical parts that keep vehicles running smoothly. The ability to create intricate, accurate parts is what makes CNC a go-to choice for automotive manufacturers. Consumer Electronics : From the sleek casing of smartphones to the sturdy frames of laptops, CNC machines are integral in producing the precision parts that make up our electronic devices. These machines help create everything from small internal components to external housings, ensuring they fit together perfectly. Medical Devices : In healthcare, where accuracy is paramount, CNC machining ensures that medical devices and equipment—like surgical instruments, implants, and diagnostic tools—are made with the utmost precision. This technology helps save lives by producing parts that meet the highest standards of quality and reliability. DIY Projects : If you're a maker or hobbyist, CNC machines can help you produce custom parts for your personal projects, whether it's a custom tool, a unique gift, or a specialized component. Why CNC Parts Are the Best Choice for Your Project Choosing CNC machining for your next project is a great decision. Whether you're looking to create a single prototype or need a batch of parts for production, CNC offers: · Unmatched Precision : CNC parts are made with extremely tight tolerances, ensuring they fit together perfectly. · Complete Customization : CNC allows you to design and create parts tailored to your specific needs, with no limitations. · Speed and Efficiency : Once set up, CNC machines can produce parts quickly, making them ideal for both small and large production runs. · Material Variety : CNC machines can work with metals, plastics, and more, giving you flexibility in material choice for your project. Wrapping Up CNC parts are at the heart of many industries and applications. Whether you're working on an automotive project, building electronic devices, or just tinkering with DIY ideas, CNC machining provides the precision and versatility you need to bring your ideas to life. It's a technology that bridges the gap between design and reality, making it possible to produce parts that are accurate, reliable, and cost-effective. If you're considering CNC for your next project, you'll find that it offers unbeatable precision, flexibility, and efficiency. So, get designing, and bring your next project to life with CNC! EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences When to Use EDM Hole Drilling When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? Limitations to Consider EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way Drilling a hole sounds simple, until you need to do it with extreme precision, into hardened materials, or to microscopic depths. That’s when you start comparing EDM hole drilling and conventional CNC drilling side by side. While both are designed to create holes, their technologies, capabilities, and ideal use cases couldn’t be more different. So, which method should you choose for your next project? Let’s dig in. What Is EDM Hole Drilling? EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) hole drilling , also called hole popping EDM or EDM deep hole drilling , uses electrical sparks to erode material. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences Feature EDM Hole Drilling CNC Drilling Material Type Conductive materials only (e.g., steel, titanium) Any machinable material Tool Contact No physical contact Direct contact via tool Hole Size Micro to medium (0.1 mm to 6 mm) Wide range (0.5 mm to 50+ mm) Tolerance Extremely tight (±0.002 mm possible) Moderate (±0.05 mm typical) Hole Depth Excellent for deep, narrow holes (30:1+ depth-to-diameter) Limited by tool rigidity and chip evacuation Speed Slower Faster for larger holes Surface Finish Very smooth, no burrs May require deburring or finishing Tool Wear Minimal due to no mechanical contact High, especially in hard materials Are you unsure about which process is right for your metal part? We can help you choose the most precise and cost-effective method for your job. Get a free quote here and let's make your design manufacturable. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Choose the Right Tool for the Hole Not every hole is created equal, and neither are the tools that make them. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options . Limitations to Consider EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way Drilling a hole sounds simple, until you need to do it with extreme precision, into hardened materials, or to microscopic depths. That’s when you start comparing EDM hole drilling and conventional CNC drilling side by side. While both are designed to create holes, their technologies, capabilities, and ideal use cases couldn’t be more different. So, which method should you choose for your next project? Let’s dig in. What Is EDM Hole Drilling? EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) hole drilling , also called hole popping EDM or EDM deep hole drilling , uses electrical sparks to erode material. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences Feature EDM Hole Drilling CNC Drilling Material Type Conductive materials only (e.g., steel, titanium) Any machinable material Tool Contact No physical contact Direct contact via tool Hole Size Micro to medium (0.1 mm to 6 mm) Wide range (0.5 mm to 50+ mm) Tolerance Extremely tight (±0.002 mm possible) Moderate (±0.05 mm typical) Hole Depth Excellent for deep, narrow holes (30:1+ depth-to-diameter) Limited by tool rigidity and chip evacuation Speed Slower Faster for larger holes Surface Finish Very smooth, no burrs May require deburring or finishing Tool Wear Minimal due to no mechanical contact High, especially in hard materials Are you unsure about which process is right for your metal part? We can help you choose the most precise and cost-effective method for your job. Get a free quote here and let's make your design manufacturable. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Choose the Right Tool for the Hole Not every hole is created equal, and neither are the tools that make them. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options .
